Quick answer: To manage arthritis, the NHS recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise weekly, strengthening exercises targeting affected joints at least twice a week, and daily flexibility work. Examples include walking, swimming, cycling, Tai Chi, and light strength training. If joints are more painful 24 hours after exercise, reduce intensity, but do not stop exercising.

NHS-Recommended Exercises for Arthritis

The NHS and NICE guidelines strongly recommend exercise as a core treatment for arthritis. Regular physical activity is as effective as painkillers for many patients — with none of the side effects.

What NICE Recommends

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends:

  • Aerobic exercise — at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week
  • Strengthening exercises — targeting muscles around affected joints, at least twice weekly
  • Flexibility work — daily stretching and range-of-motion exercises

Top NHS-Approved Exercises

Walking

The simplest and most accessible exercise. Start with 10 minutes and build up gradually. - Goal: 30 minutes, 5 days per week - Benefits: Improves cardiovascular health, supports weight management

Swimming & Aqua Aerobics

Water supports your body weight, making movement easier and less painful. - Pool temperature: Aim for 28–32°C for comfort - Benefits: Full-body workout with minimal joint impact

Cycling

Stationary or outdoor cycling strengthens leg muscles without high joint impact. - Start: 10 minutes at low resistance - Benefits: Builds quad and hamstring strength

Tai Chi

NICE specifically recommends tai chi for older adults with OA. - Frequency: 1–2 classes per week - Benefits: Improves balance, flexibility, and pain management

Strength Training

Light resistance work builds the muscles that protect joints. - Start: Bodyweight exercises (wall push-ups, chair squats) - Progress: Add resistance bands, then light weights

The 24-Hour Rule

If your joints are more painful or swollen 24 hours after exercising, you overdid it. Reduce intensity next time but do not stop entirely — rest is rarely the answer.

Where to Get Help

  • NHS Physiotherapy — ask your GP for a referral
  • NHS Fitness Studio — many leisure centres offer arthritis-specific classes
  • Versus Arthritis — free exercise guides and videos
  • Living With Arthritis — our free virtual physiotherapy programme

Reviewed by Claire Watson, MCSP, NHS Senior Physiotherapist

Practical next steps for Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises

If you came here about Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Quick questions about Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on clinically recommended arthritis exercises. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
